segments.words: Was the food very good? was the cooking good?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Yeah the cooking was pretty good but it was out of sleep in the straw stack and get up and you'd leave it to put in yes put in oh December I think there's one place that we we'd start in the morning we'd in the morning get up and start at 5 o'clock and then we would at 9 o'clock eat we'd eat breakfast before that they'd have to of course I'd be up at 4 o'clock get breakfast at 5 and the man had I guess 3.30 and they'd be eat breakfast and we'd be going at 5 and then at 9 we'd get or bring out the coffee and the sandwiches and the old donuts or something and we'd have about 20 or 30 minutes to eat and go with them and have to make it up to the night and at night you'd have to get quarter feet at noon because there was nothing from more than 1 o'clock to read yes that was kind of a rough life.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you the youngest one on the crew?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: That one? yeah quite a bit yes these other kids were about 14 or 15 they had a lot of nerves the other day yes we were all and I told them I'd come down here with my dad and my dad said I was supposed to have band and I said no they have we had to come find somebody else so that somebody made it quick or something and he would get maybe a better job not just that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you do? what work did you do after that summer? What was the work you did next?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Oh I don't know I guess the next year probably I'd go with Heaton and all these bundles there was about 10 teams and 5 bundle teams and I mean 5 pitchers and these pitchers would pitch for 2 wagons but it was kind of rough around so I might send an extra pitcher out and stick around because you'd have to ride down the upper side of the wagon and so on. It was but one of the pitchers did this they all come with a pitcher for a wagon yes 2 wagons for a pitcher and they had to ride it down higher then they would have an extra man he was dead but anyway it was you wanted your money it was a little bit yeah I could do pretty much anything on the farm yes plow from Hatterwood we all worked all horses in those days we would plow walk and plow and we were little kids big enough we'd actually game plow by 3 didn't get much done in the day because this was we were just kids you know yes because of the tract rule there now he could cut a lot of the mutters for 5 game plows yes twice that he'd have a man that night and him days he'd serve by the bush and he would get a yeah he'd plow oh 50 or 60 or 75 acres in a day and we'd plow by 5 acres in a day and spin horses and feed them a load and go out and get about 2 or 2 and a half acres and it wasn't wasn't but then a man would get $25 a day for that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you still breaking land on the place when you were young young man were you still breaking new ground?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Yeah yeah we had a big old breaking plow put more horses on and and then one would drive and the other would hold the handles.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wanted to ask you a little bit about the when you were living out there by Elk River what the logging camps were like in those days.

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Well you would they pulled mostly with donkey engines but some of them were horse they'd drag them in with horses but they would they would if they'd drag them in with with logs they would just starting taking the logs short about 30 about 30 feet or so and then you would you would load them on the logs and and haul them in and then they would cut them cut them in timbers and cut them in links they wanted so long it would be in the middle but...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What were the what were the camps like the logging camps did you get to go in them at all?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Oh yeah yes we we stood in camps they had type of cars on the camps and they had bunks on this side the bunk of mats and they run I think there was about 60 bunks on each side of the market and they had double decks on this side it was 24 bunks and but they were pretty decent places they had been clean and it was 10 hours besides walking out to your job and back from parents day half an hour and walk out and but sometimes they were if they were too far out they'd take dinner with them and maybe they they would we worked 10 hours a day and but it wasn't too big of money you had to the snow got awful deep some winter.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were most of the guys that were working there like the old time lumberjacks?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Yeah they were mostly all old lumberjacks

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What were those guys like? what do you remember them being like? the old lumberjacks.

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: All that was about our whole life they would they would come to the woods we were definitely friends and there was there was lots and lots of timber and and they were just they had their camps when they got their way off they would just move them out it was water you could get and they have a cook and a bull cook and a couple of flunkies and about 100 men and so it was yeah it was quite an improvement from the old stationer log shacks but by the time we left we left about 19 oh five years or so my oldest brother he was in the woods a lot he worked on cedar something like that pretty good work that awaited us and they they all followed timber to make poles white poles and they had big holes round towns and so on.

segments.speaker: Lola Clyde
segments.words: What nationality were most of the lumberjacks?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: A lot of Swedes among them and then about the time we were there quite a lot of the all they were pretty well mixed up and quite a lot of weeks and some of they shipped out from the old country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were there guys from Yugoslavia there too do you remember any Serbians guys from Yugoslavia?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Yes that was a mixture of all kinds yeah they hadn't just been coming out a lot couldn't even talk they couldn't some of them got rippled up too they didn't have much if they just got killed that was a lot of us too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There were a lot of accidents...

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Yeah quite a lot of accidents.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever see much fighting among lumberjacks?

segments.speaker: Gus Gamble
segments.words: Well sometimes yes sometimes we'd be fighting in the cab and so on some old Irishmen you know would get a few drinks and come in about midnight or so would they make a big disturbance yeah how you doing there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well I

segments.speaker: Lola Clyde
segments.words: Oh I was just… giving it the once over again I've forgotten so much of it I've heard this feeling that I can remember to tell you about.
